name: Illusion of transparency
statement: People overestimate how far their inner states leak out, so a lie, a rush of nerves or a flash of disgust feels visible to a room that mostly cannot see it.
meaning: The claim compares two quantities. One is how strongly a person feels something, the other is how much of it another person can actually read off their face and voice. The gap opens because the feeling is the most vivid thing in its owner's head, and the correction for the fact that nobody else has access to it is too small. Gilovich, Savitsky and Medvec call that anchoring on one's own experience and adjusting too little. A design can only test it by measuring the belief and the reality in the same room, which is why the paradigms all pair a performer with observers who are questioned separately.

origin.who: Thomas Gilovich, Kenneth Savitsky and Victoria Husted Medvec
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Their paper is "The illusion of transparency: Biased assessments of others' ability to read one's emotional states", and it named the effect and set out the anchoring account.

evidence: The 1998 paper reports three sets of studies, and its full text was read for this entry from the authors' own Cornell page through the Wayback Machine. Studies 1a, 1b and 1c show that liars overestimate the detectability of their lies. In Study 1a, 39 Cornell undergraduates played a round-robin lie detection game in groups of five. Liars guessed that 48.8% of their fellow players would pick them out, when 25.6% did, paired t(7) = 5.41, p < .001. Study 1b repeated the game with 40 students and found estimates of 50% against an actual 27%, paired t(7) = 6.56, p < .0005. The same players expected fewer others to suspect them when telling the truth, 34% against 49%, and the authors use that gap to rule out a plain self-as-target bias. Studies 2a and 2b, on 25 and 52 undergraduates, show that people believe their disgust at a foul drink is more apparent than it is. Studies 3a and 3b carry the idea into reluctance to intervene in emergencies. All three sets are read as insufficient adjustment from the anchor of one's own phenomenological experience. Savitsky and Gilovich extended the idea to public speaking in 2003, and that full text came by the same route. In Study 1, 40 Cornell students delivered extemporaneous speeches in pairs. They felt nervous at 5.95 on a scale running to ten, believed they had appeared nervous at 6.55, and were rated by their counterpart at 5.25. A follow-up with 42 Williams College students, 17 of them speakers, put speakers' self-ratings at 5.71 against observers' 4.24, t(16) = 2.94, p < .01. Study 2 gave 117 students, 77 of them speakers, a three-minute speech on race relations after being informed about the illusion, reassured, or given nothing. Observers rated the informed speakers as more composed and their speeches as better.

replication.headline: Independent samples reproduce the gap between felt and visible nerves, while two unpublished theses miss it on the lying version and on the speech-anxiety remedy, the second on 31 speakers.
replication.detail: MacInnis, Mackinnon and MacIntyre ran the speech comparison in a live classroom instead of in pairs, and describe it as a conceptual replication of the 2003 study. In an introductory public speaking course, 93 students completed the speaker surveys, and 102 had completed the trait anxiety measure beforehand. They spoke to audiences averaging 15.0 people. Speakers rated their own anxiety, rated the speech again from the imagined view of the audience, and the audience rated them on the adapted scale. Imagined audience ratings averaged 23.3 against actual audience ratings of 17.3, t(91) = 7.89, p < .001. Speakers' own anxiety averaged 24.0 and also ran above the audience, t(92) = 7.71, p < .001. Trait public speaking anxiety correlated with the paper's illusion score, r(65) = .37, p < .001, though the paper counts 66 students as having completed both measures. That score is felt anxiety minus imagined audience rating, so it is not the distance between belief and reality, and the correlation does not show that anxious speakers misjudge their audience by more. A further 36% of speakers thought the audience saw more anxiety than they had felt, which is not anxiety leaking out. The authors read that as a replication of an anomaly Savitsky and Gilovich had already met in 2003, not as a result against the effect. Rai, Mitchell and Faelling had participants read true and false episodic memories to an audience, and their abstract reports that speakers overestimated both how many listeners would think they were the liar and how many would pick the liar correctly. Their second experiment found listeners could separate lies from truths, with error. Rai, Mitchell, Kadar and Mackenzie report the same overconfidence in 13 and 14 year olds and in adults who described and lied about pictures, with adolescents no more egocentric than adults. Two unpublished theses go the other way, and both full texts were read through the Wayback Machine. Mandelbaum's dissertation ran three experiments on a lie and truth-telling game. The first two used 34 children and adolescents aged 9 to 17 and 91 undergraduates, the third 135 undergraduates. He found the illusion among truth-tellers in all three and not when participants lied, which makes it a positive finding on one half of the design rather than a flat failure. Gloth screened 543 students for fear of negative evaluation and brought 31 of the highest scorers back to give a three-minute speech after being informed about the illusion, reassured, or given no instruction. Her cells held 10, 10 and 11 speakers, no test reached significance, and the informed group's means still ran in the predicted direction on every measure. That is an underpowered miss on the 2003 remedy rather than a failure of the illusion.

study.cite: MacInnis, C. C., Mackinnon, S. P., & MacIntyre, P. D. (2010). The illusion of transparency and normative beliefs about anxiety during public speaking. Current Research in Social Psychology, 15(4), 42-52.

limits: The search behind this verdict covered Crossref, PubMed, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, the publisher pages for both founding papers, and web searches for preregistered, multi-laboratory and registered-report replications, last run on 21 September 2026. No Many Labs project and no registered report on this effect came up. Neither founding paper is open access at its publisher, but both versions of record were served from the authors' Cornell page through the Wayback Machine, so the figures above are taken from the papers themselves. Both theses were served the same way after their repositories answered a direct request with a Cloudflare challenge. No standardised effect size is reported in either founding paper, and none is calculated here. The abstract of the 2014 adolescent study was read through Semantic Scholar's record rather than at Springer, which served only the reference list, and the two Rai papers have not been opened in full. The two dissenting results are a master's thesis and a doctoral dissertation, neither peer reviewed, and the thesis rested on 31 speakers against the 77 of the study it repeats. Brown and Stopa took a different route, asking participants to rate both illusions after a memory task under low and high social evaluation, and found transparency rated above the spotlight effect in the low condition and the order reversed in the high one. That measures how the two feelings move, not the distance between belief and reality, so it is not a test of the gap.
misreadings: The effect is not the spotlight effect, which has its own entry at 22. The spotlight effect is about how much others notice one's actions and appearance; this is about how much they can read one's inner state. Gilovich and Savitsky set the pair side by side in 1999 as two egocentric assessments, and Brown and Stopa found them moving in opposite directions as social pressure rose. The finding is also passed on as an assurance that nothing shows at all. Rai and colleagues report that listeners could tell lies from truths, so the honest summary is overestimation rather than invisibility. The therapeutic version runs ahead of the evidence in the same way. Savitsky and Gilovich's Study 2 found that telling speakers about the illusion improved their speeches, and the one attempt to repeat that, on 31 speakers selected for fear of negative evaluation, did not. The last trap is the direction of the error. Speakers in the 2003 study rated themselves as looking more nervous than they felt, which runs against the leakage account, and the authors flag it in a footnote as anomalous. A later classroom study found the same thing in 36% of its speakers. Anyone citing that as fresh dissent is citing something the original already reported.
